top.line: Vibe coding should be called explorer coding instead
top.para: Building with agents is the best thing since the spreadsheet, and what it produces is a better brief than any document. Explorer is Wardley's word for it. An explorer-coded app is not ready to be in line: villagers must maintain it and town planners own it, and every product should offer an explorer version.

in-short.line: Explorer-coded apps are briefs, not yet products
in-short.para: What people call vibe coding is exploration, with a fast feedback loop like the spreadsheet's, and it produces a working brief. Once others depend on it, it needs villagers and town planners. Towards commodity there are fewer agents in line, and products should sell conversions from an explorer version.

name.line: Vibe coding demeans the work; explorer coding names it
name.para: Karpathy coined vibe coding in February 2025 for throwaway projects, and it became Collins' word of the year, but it suggests ad-libbing; Andrew Ng called AI coding a deeply intellectual exercise. Wardley's explorers chart uncharted land and fail a lot. Exploratory programming is the nearest prior term.

spreadsheet.line: Fast feedback makes this the best thing since spreadsheets
spreadsheet.para: Spreadsheets won through instant feedback, and anything beyond them used to mean writing a document and waiting; now the loop is fast for apps, workflows and product customisations. Someone in HR, hearing what her team could build, asked when she could start. A working app is the best brief.

in-line.line: An explorer-coded app is not ready for production
in-line.para: It may look like an application, but nobody has read the code, validated the architecture or checked it against standards. Dependence comes quickly: once people rely on it, even one person, it is mission critical and must be maintained, checked and kept working across versions.

handover.line: Villagers maintain explorer apps; town planners own the code
handover.para: Villagers add tests, safe releases, agent behaviour policies and data rules. Town planners take ownership and accountability, as the Linux kernel and Fedora already require of whoever submits code. Explorers cannot be accountable for unread code, and the nearer commodity, the fewer agents in line and the more deterministic code.

products.line: Every product should have a paid-conversion explorer version
products.para: Users would reshape a product by talking to it and keep their version, then pay to convert it into a maintained villager product or a properly built town planner product. Each step is revenue and tells the vendor what users want. The same path fits companies and open-source projects.

limits.line: The term and the product model are both proposals
limits.para: No established use of explorer coding was found; exploratory programming is its ancestor. Explorer-coded apps are briefs, not good code. The HR conversation is one illustration, not a survey, and no known vendor sells an explorer version of its product.

sources.line: Sources: Karpathy, Ng, Wardley and kernel AI policies
sources.para: A voice memo of 16 October 2026. Andrej Karpathy's post of 2 February 2025 via Wikipedia, Andrew Ng via Business Insider, Simon Wardley on explorers, villagers and town planners, Kery and Myers on exploratory programming, the Linux kernel's AI coding assistant rules and Fedora's AI contributions proposal.
